words.definition: The art of speaking well in public to move or impress a crowd.
words.example: Her closing argument was a masterpiece of oratory that left the jury spellbound.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'oral' + 'story' — telling a story out loud with power.

words.definition: A method of examining truth through logical argument between opposing viewpoints.
words.example: Through careful dialectic, the two philosophers refined each other's positions into a sharper truth.
words.mnemonic: 'dia-' (across) + 'lect' (speak): speaking across two sides to reach truth.

words.definition: To make someone agree or act by offering reasons or appeals.
words.example: It took an hour, but she finally persuaded her father to lend her the car.
words.mnemonic: per- (thoroughly) + 'suave' — sweet-talk someone all the way to yes.

words.definition: To gently and patiently urge someone toward doing what you want.
words.example: She coaxed the frightened kitten out from under the porch with a saucer of milk.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'coke's' — offer someone a Coke to gently win them over.

words.definition: To coax someone with flattery, teasing, or sweet promises.
words.example: He cajoled his sister into covering his chores by promising to wash her car.
words.mnemonic: ca-JOLE sounds like 'jolly' — jolly someone along with charm until they give in.

words.definition: To ask someone earnestly and humbly for something you badly want.
words.example: The refugees entreated the guards to let their children cross the border first.
words.mnemonic: en- + 'treat' — beg someone to treat you kindly.

words.definition: To beg someone urgently and emotionally for help or mercy.
words.example: 'Please don't go,' she implored, gripping his sleeve as the train pulled in.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'I'm poor' — a beggar pleading desperately for help.

words.definition: To beg someone eagerly and anxiously to do something.
words.example: The villagers beseeched the king to spare their harvest from the heavy tax.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'be-seek' — you seek help so hard that you beg for it.

words.definition: To strongly urge or encourage someone to make an effort.
words.example: The coach exhorted his exhausted players to push through the final minutes.
words.mnemonic: 'egg-zort' — egg someone on toward a great effort.

words.definition: To stir someone from rest or calm into strong feeling or action.
words.example: The general's speech roused the weary troops to charge one more time.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'house' — a fire alarm rouses the whole house awake.

words.definition: To fill someone with the urge or confidence to do something great.
words.example: The teacher's own love of science inspired half her students to become engineers.
words.mnemonic: in- + 'spire' (breath, as in respire) — to breathe energy and ideas into someone.

words.definition: To give someone a reason or drive to take action.
words.example: The promise of a bonus motivated the team to finish the project a week early.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'motive' and 'motor' — a motive is the motor that drives you.

words.definition: To influence someone's opinion or make it lean one way.
words.example: A single tearful witness swayed the undecided jurors toward acquittal.
words.mnemonic: Picture a tree swaying in wind — arguments make your opinion lean and swing.

words.definition: To get something by using soft flattery and coaxing words.
words.example: The child wheedled an extra scoop of ice cream from his doting grandmother.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'needle' — you gently needle and sweet-talk until they give in.

words.definition: To prove stronger and win out, or to successfully urge someone to agree.
words.example: She finally prevailed upon her reluctant boss to approve the extra vacation days.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'vail' like 'valiant' — the valiant side proves stronger and wins.

words.definition: To publicly support or argue in favor of a particular cause or policy.
words.example: She advocates for cleaner rivers at every town council meeting.
words.mnemonic: ad- + Latin 'vocare' (to call): you 'call out' on behalf of a cause.

words.definition: To actively fight for, defend, or promote a person or cause.
words.example: He championed workers' rights long before it was popular to do so.
words.mnemonic: A prize-fighting champion steps into the ring to battle for someone's side.

words.definition: To adopt and give loyal support to a belief, cause, or way of life.
words.example: The senator openly espouses stricter limits on factory emissions.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spouse' — you marry yourself to an idea and stay faithful to it.

words.definition: To put forward an idea or theory for others to consider.
words.example: The scientist propounded a bold theory about the planet's origin.
words.mnemonic: pro- (forward) + 'pound': you pound your idea forward onto the table for debate.

words.definition: To make something easier to understand by removing confusion or vagueness.
words.example: Could you clarify what you meant when you said the deadline was 'flexible'?
words.mnemonic: 'clear' + -ify: literally to make clear.

words.definition: To make an idea plain using examples, pictures, or comparisons.
words.example: He used a simple graph to illustrate how quickly the debt had grown.
words.mnemonic: Hidden Latin 'lustrare' (to light up): to shine light on an idea.

words.definition: To show clearly that something is true or how it works through evidence or action.
words.example: The instructor demonstrated how to tie the knot step by step.
words.mnemonic: A 'demo' demonstrates — it shows you exactly how the thing works.

words.definition: To invent logical-sounding excuses for behavior really driven by other motives.
words.example: He rationalized skipping the gym by insisting the walk to work was enough.
words.mnemonic: 'rational' + -ize: you dress up a choice to make it seem reasonable after the fact.

words.definition: To respond to an argument or action with an opposing one.
words.example: She countered his objection with fresh data from the study.
words.mnemonic: A boxer's counter-punch: you hit back the moment your opponent strikes.

words.definition: To argue against the truth or validity of something.
words.example: The two families disputed the ownership of the land for years.
words.mnemonic: dis- (against) + Latin 'putare' (to think): to think against what someone claims.

words.definition: To announce something officially or publicly with great emphasis.
words.example: The king proclaimed a national holiday from the palace balcony.
words.mnemonic: pro- (forth) + 'claim': you claim it forth, loudly, for everyone to hear.

words.definition: To declare something formally, or to make the sound of a word.
words.example: The judge pronounced the defendant not guilty, and the courtroom erupted.
words.mnemonic: pro- + Latin 'nuntiare' (to announce): to announce a verdict or a sound officially.

words.definition: Using inflated, pompous language that sounds impressive but means little.
words.example: His bombastic victory speech was crammed with grand phrases and empty promises.
words.mnemonic: Think 'bomb-blast': loud explosions of big words that leave nothing behind.

words.definition: Marked by lofty, showy speech intended to impress listeners.
words.example: The professor's grandiloquent lecture left students dazzled but no wiser.
words.mnemonic: 'grand' + 'eloquent': grandness of speech pushed way past good taste.

words.definition: Trying to appear more important, talented, or cultured than is actually true.
words.example: The café's pretentious menu described plain toast as 'artisanal grain craft.'
words.mnemonic: Contains 'pretend': you're pretending to be grander than you really are.

words.definition: Full of elaborate flourishes and showy decoration, especially in style, language, or a ruddy complexion.
words.example: His florid prose was so crammed with flourishes that readers lost the actual point.
words.mnemonic: Florid sounds like 'floral' — picture over-decorated writing smothered in blossoms.

words.definition: Elaborately decorated with complex, showy detail.
words.example: The ornate ceiling dripped with gold leaf, carved cherubs, and swirling plasterwork.
words.mnemonic: Ornate contains 'ornament' — imagine a room buried under ornaments.

words.definition: Expressing much meaning briefly and forcefully in few words.
words.example: Her pithy one-liner said more than the speaker's hour-long lecture.
words.mnemonic: Pith is the concentrated core of a stem — pithy speech is all core, no filler.

words.definition: Talking easily, freely, and at great length.
words.example: So voluble was the guide that she barely paused for breath during the entire tour.
words.mnemonic: Voluble sounds like 'volume' — a person whose volume of words never shuts off.

words.definition: Feeling or showing intense, passionate emotion.
words.example: The candidate's fervid supporters chanted late into the night, hoarse but tireless.
words.mnemonic: Fervid shares a root with 'fervent' and 'fever' — a feverish heat of feeling.

words.definition: Refusing to change one's mind or course despite good reasons.
words.example: The stubborn toddler folded his arms and flatly refused to leave the playground.
words.mnemonic: Picture a stubborn tree stub in the ground — you can push all day and it won't budge.

words.definition: Strongly favoring one party, cause, or group over all others.
words.example: The debate collapsed into partisan bickering, each side cheering only its own team.
words.mnemonic: Partisan contains 'part' — someone who always takes the part of one side.

words.definition: Unfairly favoring one side, person, or viewpoint over another.
words.example: The referee seemed biased, awarding every close call to the home team.
words.mnemonic: In lawn bowling, a 'bias' is a weight that makes the ball curve one way — biased judgment always curves.

words.definition: Treating all sides equally without favoring anyone.
words.example: As an impartial judge, she weighed both arguments carefully before ruling.
words.mnemonic: Im- (not) + partial — literally 'not taking a part' or side.

words.definition: Based on facts and evidence rather than personal feelings or opinions.
words.example: The report stuck to objective measurements: temperatures, distances, and dated timestamps.
words.mnemonic: An 'object' is a real thing out in the world — objective means grounded in external facts.

words.definition: Based on personal feelings, tastes, or opinions rather than outside facts.
words.example: Beauty is subjective — the painting that moved her left him completely cold.
words.mnemonic: The 'subject' is the person perceiving — subjective is filtered through one mind.

words.definition: An unfair opinion formed before knowing the facts.
words.example: Her prejudice against the neighborhood vanished once she actually lived there.
words.mnemonic: Pre- (before) + judice (judge) — to judge before you know anything.

words.definition: Biased information spread to promote a cause or damage an opponent.
words.example: Wartime posters were pure propaganda, painting the enemy as monstrous and cowardly.
words.mnemonic: Propaganda 'propagates' — it spreads a one-sided message like fast-growing weeds.

words.definition: A leader who wins support by stirring emotions and prejudices instead of reason.
words.example: The demagogue whipped the crowd into fury with scapegoats and empty promises.
words.mnemonic: Greek demos (people) + agogos (leader) — but the kind who manipulates the mob.

words.definition: Logically connected, clear, and easy to follow.
words.example: After a coffee, her scattered notes finally formed a coherent argument.
words.mnemonic: Co- (together) + here (stick) — coherent thoughts all stick together.

words.definition: Easy to understand and expressed in a clear, coherent way.
words.example: Despite her high fever, she gave a lucid account of exactly what had happened that night.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'lux' (light) — a lucid explanation sheds light on a murky topic.

words.definition: To disguise or conceal one's true feelings, motives, or beliefs.
words.example: He tried to dissemble his disappointment, forcing a cheerful smile for the cameras.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'disassemble' — you take the truth apart and hide the pieces.

words.definition: To invent a false story or make up information in order to deceive.
words.example: The witness was caught fabricating an alibi that the security footage clearly disproved.
words.mnemonic: A 'fabric' is woven from threads — you weave a whole story out of nothing.

words.definition: To add extra, often untrue or fancy details to make something more appealing.
words.example: Grandpa loved to embellish his war stories, adding a new hero every time he told them.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'bell' — hang pretty bells on a plain tale to dress it up.

words.definition: To describe something as bigger, better, or worse than it really is.
words.example: When he claimed he had waited a thousand years in that line, he was surely exaggerating.
words.mnemonic: 'Ex-AGGER-ate' — aggregate piles everything up far past its real size.

words.definition: A figure of speech using extreme overstatement for emphasis, not meant literally.
words.example: Saying 'I've told you a million times' is pure hyperbole, not an actual tally.
words.mnemonic: 'Hyper + bowl' — a hyperactive bowl overflowing way past the rim.

words.definition: A mild or indirect word used in place of one considered harsh or blunt.
words.example: 'Passed away' is a gentle euphemism people reach for instead of saying 'died.'
words.mnemonic: Greek 'eu' (good) + 'pheme' (speech) — good-sounding speech for an ugly thing.

words.definition: Specialized words used by a particular profession or group, hard for outsiders.
words.example: The lawyers' jargon left the jury baffled by terms like 'tortfeasor' and 'estoppel.'
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'jar-gone' — the meaning is sealed in a jar, gone to outsiders.

words.definition: An indirect hint or sly remark suggesting something, usually negative or improper.
words.example: She never accused him outright, but her innuendo left everyone suspecting the worst.
words.mnemonic: 'In-you-end-o' — a hint that slips in at the end, never stated straight.

words.definition: An indirect or passing reference to a person, event, or work of art.
words.example: Calling the overgrown garden 'an Eden' was an allusion to the biblical paradise.
words.mnemonic: Unlike 'illusion,' an allusion a-LU-des — points away to something already known.

words.definition: A short, often amusing account of a real incident or person.
words.example: To break the ice, she opened her speech with an anecdote about her disastrous first job.
words.mnemonic: 'Anec-dote' sounds like 'antidote' — a little story to cure a dull moment.

words.definition: A response that argues against and tries to disprove a previous claim.
words.example: After the prosecutor's charge, the defense offered a sharp rebuttal pointing to the timeline.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-BUT-tal' — the 'but...' that pushes straight back against an argument.

words.definition: Something granted or admitted, especially a point yielded in an argument.
words.example: As a concession to the strikers, management agreed to shorten the weekend shifts.
words.mnemonic: To 'concede' is to cede (give up) ground; the concession is the ground handed over.

words.definition: To provoke or prod someone into action, often by teasing or annoying them.
words.example: His rivals goaded him into taking the dangerous jump by calling him a coward.
words.mnemonic: A 'goad' is a pointed stick for driving cattle — you poke someone into moving.

words.definition: To ask for or try to obtain something from someone.
words.example: The charity volunteers stood outside the station to solicit donations from commuters.
words.mnemonic: 'So-LI-cit' — think of a solicitor (lawyer) who is always asking you for things.

words.definition: A quick, sharp, and often witty reply, especially one that turns criticism back on its speaker.
words.example: When he mocked her cooking, she shot back a retort so cutting the whole table went silent.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'RE-TORT' — you 'torque' the insult back, twisting the other person's words to fling them in return.

words.definition: To deliberately win someone's favor or approval through flattery and eager, pleasing behavior.
words.example: The new intern tried to ingratiate himself with the boss by laughing loudly at every joke and fetching her coffee unasked.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'in-GRATIA-te' — Latin 'gratia' means favor or grace, so you work your way INTO someone's good GRACES.

words.definition: Intended to teach or instruct, sometimes in an overbearing, moralizing way.
words.example: The film's story stalled whenever a character paused to deliver a didactic little speech about honesty.
words.mnemonic: 'DIDACT-ic' shares its root with the Greek 'didaskein', to teach — picture a stern professor whose every sentence is a lesson.
